claim: Preclinical and clinical studies show that mild to moderate hypothermia is neuroprotective in sudden cardiac arrest, ischemic stroke, perinatal hypoxia/ischemia, traumatic brain injury, and seizures.
source: Preclinical and clinical studies show that mild to moderate hypothermia is neuroprotective in sudden cardiac arrest, ischemic stroke, perinatal hypoxia/ischemia, traumatic brain injury, and seizures.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research (Kida et al., 2013; Andresen et al., 2015; Sartorius and Berger, 1998; Schmitt et al., 2006; Niquet et al., 2015a; Niquet et al., 2015b; Karkar et al., 2002; Kim et al., 2017) as indicated in the full text.

claim: Neurotensin (NT) is a 13 amino acid neuropeptide that regulates body temperature.
source: Neurotensin (NT), a 13 amino acid neuropeptide that regulates body temperature
evidence: Supported by citations (Coquerel et al., 1988; Coquerel et al., 1986; Fanelli et al., 2015) as indicated in the full text.

claim: NT induces pharmacologically induced hypothermia (PIH) when administered intracerebrally.
source: NT induces PIH when administered intracerebrally.
evidence: Supported by citations (Coquerel et al., 1986; Coquerel et al., 1988; Popp et al., 2007; Fanelli et al., 2015) as indicated in the full text.

claim: NT does not induce hypothermia when administered peripherally due to its rapid degradation and poor passage of the blood-brain barrier (BBB).
source: However, these effects are not observed if NT is administered peripherally, due to its rapid degradation and poor passage of the blood-brain barrier (BBB).
evidence: Supported by citations (McMahon et al., 2002; Gordon et al., 2003; Orwig et al., 2009; Boules et al., 2013) as indicated in the full text.

claim: VH-N412 displayed improved stability, binding potential to both the LDLR and NTSR-1, rodent/human cross-reactivity and improved brain distribution.
source: One of these conjugates, VH-N412, displayed improved stability, binding potential to both the LDLR and NTSR-1, rodent/human cross-reactivity and improved brain distribution.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript including SPR, binding assays, stability assays, and brain perfusion studies.

claim: VH-N412 elicited rapid hypothermia associated with anticonvulsant effects in a mouse model of kainate (KA)-induced status epilepticus (SE).
source: In a mouse model of kainate (KA)-induced status epilepticus (SE), VH-N412 elicited rapid hypothermia associated with anticonvulsant effects
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and described in the Results section.

claim: VH-N412 induced potent neuroprotection in the hippocampus 7 days following SE.
source: Seven days following SE, we observed potent neuroprotection and reduced inflammation in the hippocampus
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4, 5, and 6 including FJC staining and NeuN immunohistochemistry.

claim: VH-N412 reduced hippocampal inflammation 7 days following SE.
source: Seven days following SE, we observed potent neuroprotection and reduced inflammation in the hippocampus
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6 including GFAP and Iba1 immunohistochemistry.

claim: VH-N412 reduced sprouting of the dentate gyrus mossy fibers assessed 2 months after SE.
source: Neuroprotection elicited by VH-N412 also reduced significantly aberrant sprouting of the dentate gyrus (DG) mossy fibers assessed 2 months after SE
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7 using ZnT-3 immunohistochemistry.

claim: VH-N412 preserved learning and memory skills in mice treated after SE.
source: preserved learning and memory skills in the treated mice
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8 using the olfactory tubing maze test.

claim: NTSR1 is expressed in hippocampal pyramidal neurons in vitro and in vivo, in cell bodies, dendrites, and spines.
source: We showed that NTSR1, one of the NT receptors, was expressed in hippocampal pyramidal neurons in vitro and in vivo, in cell bodies, dendrites, and spines, the postsynaptic compartment of glutamatergic synapses.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 10, 11, and 12 using immunocytochemistry and immunohistochemistry.

claim: VH-N412 displayed temperature-independent neuroprotective properties in cultured hippocampal neurons challenged with neurotoxic NMDA or KA glutamate agonists.
source: we show in cultured hippocampal neurons challenged with neurotoxic NMDA or KA glutamate agonists that VH-N412 displayed temperature-independent neuroprotective properties
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 13 using in vitro neuronal survival assays.

claim: VH-N412 neuroprotective effects in vitro are as potent as oestradiol or BDNF.
source: VH-N412 displayed temperature-independent neuroprotective properties that are as potent as oestradiol or BDNF.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 13 comparing VH-N412 to oestradiol and BDNF in neuronal survival assays.

claim: VH-N21 induced a transient and mild hypothermia that was dose-dependent and reached a maximum of –3.7°C 1 hr after injection at a dose of 8 mg/kg molar equivalent NT.
source: VH-N21 induced a transient and mild hypothermia, that was dose-dependent and that reached a maximum of –3.7°C 1 hr after injection, with a dose of 8 mg/kg molar equivalent NT (eq. NT).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Native NT at the same dose as VH-N21 did not induce significant hypothermia.
source: In contrast, no significant hypothermia was observed with native NT at the same dose (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: VH-N41 induced a stronger and more sustained hypothermia after i.v. injection in mice, with a maximal body temperature decrease of –6.8°C.
source: the resulting VH-N41 conjugate (Figure 1C) induced a stronger and more sustained hypothermia after i.v. injection in mice, with a maximal body temperature decrease of –6.8°C (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: VH-N412 elicited a hypothermic response with a maximal body temperature decrease of –6.4°C.
source: this VH-N412 conjugate elicited a hypothermic response similar to that of VH-N41, with a maximal body temperature decrease of –6.4°C, but with an even more sustained profile (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The control PEG6-NT(8–13) compound showed no hypothermic effect.
source: No effect was observed with the control PEG6-NT(8–13) compound, confirming the involvement of the VH4129 peptide in the hypothermic effect of VH-N412.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: VH-N412 displayed an ED50 of 0.69 mg/kg eq. NT.
source: Dose-response curves confirmed that VH-N412 displayed an ED50 similar to that of VH-N41, estimated at 0.69 and 0.93 eq. NT, respectively (corresponding to 0.80 and 1.67 mg/kg, respectively) (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: VH-N412 retains binding potential to human LDLR with an affinity of 63.8 nM.
source: This was confirmed using surface plasmon resonance (SPR) on immobilized human LDLR, with free VH4129 and the VH-N412 conjugate displaying very similar binding affinity and profiles, namely 72.6 and 63.8 nM, respectively (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A using SPR.

claim: VH-N412 binds to rat NTSR-1 with a Ki in the low nanomolar range.
source: Both NT(1–13) and VH-N412 showed similar Ki values for rNTSR-1 and hNTSR-1, in the low nanomolar range (Figure 2B, right and left graphs).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B using binding competition assays.

claim: VH-N412 binds to human NTSR-1 with a Ki in the low nanomolar range.
source: Both NT(1–13) and VH-N412 showed similar Ki values for rNTSR-1 and hNTSR-1, in the low nanomolar range (Figure 2B, right and left graphs).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B using binding competition assays.

claim: Native NT has a very low resistance in mouse blood with a half-life of 9 minutes.
source: As opposed to the very low resistance of the native NT (t1/2 of 9 min), both VH-NT conjugates showed greatly enhanced stability
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: VH-N412 has an in vitro half-life of 83 minutes in mouse blood.
source: with VH-N412 showing the highest in vitro half-life estimated at 83 min, compared to 44 min with VH-N21 (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: VH-N412 has an in vitro half-life of 74 minutes in human blood.
source: The in vitro half-life of VH-N412 was estimated at 74 min in human blood, demonstrating similar metabolic resistance across species (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: VH-N412 showed a BBB transport rate clearance (Kin) of 0.37 µL/s/g of brain tissue.
source: In contrast, VH-N21 and VH-N412 showed Kin values of 0.13 and 0.37 µL/s/g respectively (Figure 2E)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E using in situ brain perfusion.

claim: Native NT demonstrated a very low BBB transport with a Kin of approximately 0.04 µL/s/g of brain tissue.
source: NT demonstrated a very low BBB transport, with a Kin of ~0.04 µL/s/g of brain tissue (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E using in situ brain perfusion.

claim: VH-N412 did not alter the integrity of the BBB.
source: Furthermore, VH-N412 did not alter the integrity of the BBB. Indeed, the brain distribution volume of 14C-sucrose as a marker of brain vascular volume in VH-N412 mice (19.00±1.00 µL/g) was in the normal range (i.e. Vvasc <20.00 µL/g) (Cattelotte et al., 2008) and similar to that of NT (18.00±2.00 µL/g).
evidence: Supported by experimental data using 14C-sucrose as a BBB integrity marker.

claim: VH-N412 administered at the dose of 4 mg/kg eq. NT 30 min after SE onset led to transient hypothermia.
source: VH-N412 administered at the dose of 4 mg/kg eq. NT 30 min after SE onset (SE30), hence 2.5 hr after s.c. administration of KA (KA-2H), invariably led to transient hypothermia (Figure 3B; Supplementary file 3)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Mean decreases in body temperature of –2.12°C were recorded at SE30 for SE+VH-N412 animals compared to SE animals.
source: Mean decreases in body temperature of –2.12°C were recorded at SE30 for SE+VH-N412 animals (36.50 ± 0.34°C, p<0.01, Tukey's test) as compared to SE animals (38.00 ± 0.37°C) (Figure 3B; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and statistical analysis.

claim: VH-N412 was associated with a significant decrease of seizures in the SE+VH-N412 group at SE30 compared with the SE group.
source: This hypothermia was associated with a significant decrease of seizures in the SE+VH-N412 group (1.97±0.36, p<0.01, Tukey's test) at SE30 as compared with the SE group (5.38±0.15) (Figure 3C; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and statistical analysis.

claim: SE+VH-N412 animals presented an average seizure intensity score of 2 or less during SE30-SE150 min.
source: SE+VH-N412 animals presented an average of seizure intensity score of 2 or less during the rest of the experiment (SE30-SE150 min).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Diazepam (DZP) at 15 mg/kg induced hypothermia in SE+DZP animals.
source: significant hypothermia was also observed in these animals at all time points (Figure 3B and C; Supplementary file 3 and 4; p<0.01, Tukey's test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: NT8–13 administered at SE30 showed no significant variations of body temperature compared with SE animals.
source: No significant variations of body temperature or seizure intensity score were observed when NT8–13 was administered at SE30, as compared with SE animals at all time points (Figure 3B and C; Supplementary files 3 and 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: FJC staining is significantly increased in CA1 of SE animals compared to SHAM animals.
source: Semiquantitative analysis revealed that FJC staining is significantly increased in CA1 (222.73 ± 11.80%, 123%, p<0.01, Tukey's test)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: FJC staining is significantly increased in CA3 of SE animals compared to SHAM animals.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: FJC staining is significantly increased in the Hilus of SE animals compared to SHAM animals.
source: and to a lesser extent in H (120 ± 4.98%, 20%, p<0.05, Tukey's test) of SE animals compared to SHAM animals
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: No difference in FJC staining was found in the GCL between SE and SHAM animals.
source: No difference in FJC staining was found in the GCL (100 ± 5.44%; n=3 mice; p>0.05; ANOVA) (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Neural cell degeneration observed in SE animals was significantly decreased when VH-N412 was administered at SE30.
source: Neural cell degeneration observed in SE animals was significantly decreased when VH-N412 was administered at SE30 (CA1: 97.97 ± 2.60%; CA3: 109.58 ± 7.31%; H: 89.82 ± 3.20%; p<0.01, Tukey's test) (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: No changes in FJC staining were observed when NT8-13 was administered at SE30.
source: In contrast, no changes were observed when NT8-13 was administered (CA1: 222.59 ± 12.02%; CA3: 200.08 ± 11.84%; H: 100.98 ± 5.75%; p>0.05; ANOVA) (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: SE animals displayed a decreased NeuN staining and significantly increased neuronal death score in the hippocampal formation compared to SHAM animals.
source: SE animals displayed a decreased NeuN staining and significantly increased neuronal death score in the hippocampal formation compared to SHAM animals.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: When VH-N412 was administered at SE30, the neuronal death score was significantly reduced by 51%.
source: When VH-N412 or DZP was administered at SE30, the neuronal death score was significantly reduced by 51% and 34% respectively (p<0.01, Tukey's test; Figure 6B, left histogram).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: When DZP was administered at SE30, the neuronal death score was significantly reduced by 34%.
source: When VH-N412 or DZP was administered at SE30, the neuronal death score was significantly reduced by 51% and 34% respectively (p<0.01, Tukey's test; Figure 6B, left histogram).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: No changes in neuronal death score were observed when NT8-13 was administered at SE30.
source: However, no changes were observed when NT8-13 was administered (p>0.05; ANOVA) (Figure 6B, left histogram).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In SE animals, a significant activation of glial cells occurred in all hippocampal areas.
source: In SE animals, a significant activation of glial cells occurred in all hippocampal areas (GFAP: 277.74 ± 37.96%, 178%; p<0.01, Tukey's test; Figure 6B, middle histogram; Iba1: 440.04 ± 29.86%, 340%; p<0.01, Tukey's test; Figure 6B, right histogram).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B using GFAP and Iba1 immunolabeling.

claim: The inflammatory response was significantly decreased when VH-N412 was administered at SE30.
source: This inflammatory response was significantly decreased when VH-N412 was administered at SE30 (GFAP: 96.44 ± 4.48%; 181.50%; p<0.01, Tukey's test; Figure 6B, middle histogram; Iba1: 257.69 ± 16.96%, 182.31%; p<0.01, Tukey's test; Figure 6B, right histogram)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The inflammatory response was significantly decreased when DZP was administered at SE30.
source: or DZP (GFAP: 56.32 ± 6.61%; 221.41%; p<0.01, Tukey's test; Figure 6B, middle histogram; Iba1: 164.59 ± 4.88%, 275.41%; p<0.01, Tukey's test; Figure 6B, right histogram).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: No significant changes in inflammatory response were observed when NT(8–13) was administered at SE30.
source: No significant changes were observed when NT(8–13) was administered at SE30 (GFAP: 316.87 ± 24.36%; p>0.05; ANOVA; Figure 6B, middle histogram; Iba1: 383.32 ± 40.40%; p>0.05; ANOVA; Figure 6B, right histogram).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In SE animals, mossy fiber terminals were observed within the IML and GCL of the DG.
source: In SE animals, mossy fiber terminals were not only observed in the hilar region as in SHAM mice, but also within the IML and GCL of the DG (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A using ZnT-3 immunohistochemistry.

claim: The number of mossy fiber terminals innervating the IML was significantly reduced in animals administered with VH-N412 at SE30 compared to SE animals.
source: In comparison with SE animals (50.38±15.57), the number of terminals innervating the IML was significantly reduced in animals administered with VH-N412 at SE30 (7.79±2.54, 84.53%; p<0.01, Tukey's test, Figure 7B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The number of mossy fiber terminals innervating the IML was not significantly different when NT(8–13) was administered at SE30.
source: but was not significantly different when NT(8–13) (25.85±6.39; p>0.05; ANOVA) was administered at SE30 (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: SE mice reached a significantly lower percentage of correct responses in the OTM test compared to SHAM and SE+VH-N412 groups.
source: Post hoc analysis using the Newman-Keuls test revealed that SE mice reached a significantly lower percentage of correct responses in comparison with the two other groups (p<0.05).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B using the olfactory tubing maze test.

claim: A significant difference in percentage of correct responses was observed starting from the third training session between SE and SE+VH-N412 groups.
source: Selective ANOVAs showed a significant difference starting from the third training session between SE and SE+VH-N412 groups (ANOVAs: F(1,14) ≥ 5.12; p<0.05).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B and statistical analysis.

claim: SE mice exhibited a strong hyperactivity in comparison with SHAM mice in the open field test.
source: SE mice exhibited a strong hyperactivity in comparison with SHAM mice. The average distances covered by mice from these two groups were significantly different on the first session of 5 min (ANOVA: F(1,14) = 29.56; p<0.001) and on the total of the two sessions (ANOVA: F(1,14) = 11.18; p<0.01).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C using the open field test.

claim: Treatment of SE mice with VH-N412 maintained a locomotor activity similar to SHAM mice.
source: Treatment of SE mice with VH-N412 maintained a locomotor activity similar to SHAM mice on the two successive sessions (ANOVAs: F(1,18) ≤ 0.24; ns) and significantly lower than untreated SE mice on each of the two sessions of 5 min (ANOVAs: F(1,14) ≥ 5.92; p<0.05) (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: VH-N412 did not modulate KA-induced neuronal hyperactivity in hippocampal slices.
source: When VH-N412 was applied at increasing doses of 0.1, 1, and 10 μM over a 30 min period, the KA-induced increase in firing rate in CA1 did not change significantly.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1 using multielectrode array recordings.

claim: VH-N412 treatment increased the expression of RBM3 mRNA at 16 hr in the hippocampus compared to control mice.
source: RT-qPCR analysis normalized with GAPDH on pooled samples (three animals per time point) showed significant increase of mRNA encoding RBM3 (2.86±0.33, 3-fold) and CIRBP (1.53±0.56, 1.5-fold) relative to PBS injected control (1.00±0.00) at the 16 and 8 hr time points, respectively (Dunnett's test, p<0.05) (Figure 9A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9A using RT-qPCR.

claim: VH-N412 treatment increased the expression of CIRBP mRNA at 8 hr in the hippocampus compared to control mice.
source: RT-qPCR analysis normalized with GAPDH on pooled samples (three animals per time point) showed significant increase of mRNA encoding RBM3 (2.86±0.33, 3-fold) and CIRBP (1.53±0.56, 1.5-fold) relative to PBS injected control (1.00±0.00) at the 16 and 8 hr time points, respectively (Dunnett's test, p<0.05) (Figure 9A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9A using RT-qPCR.

claim: VH-N412 treatment resulted in significant increase of RBM3 protein levels at 4, 8, and 16 hr in the hippocampus.
source: Results showed significant increase of RBM3 protein levels (4 hr: 270.88 ± 5.12%, 2.7-fold, Dunnett's test, p<0.05; 8 hr: 465.74 ± 70.05%, 4.65-fold Dunnett's test, p<0.001; 16 hr: 251.97 ± 49.34%, 2.5-fold, Dunnett's test, p<0.05)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9B using western blot.

claim: VH-N412 treatment resulted in significant increase of CIRBP protein levels at 4 hr in the hippocampus.
source: and CIRBP protein levels (4 hr: 235.15 ± 13.02%, 2.35-fold, Dunnett's test, p<0.001) relative to PBS injected control (100.00 ± 0.00%) (Figure 9B, Figure 9—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9B using western blot.

claim: VH-N412 did not regulate RBM3 and CIRBP mRNA at all concentrations used in cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: Our results showed that cultured neurons treated with VH-N412 did not display significant differences of RBM3 and CIRBP mRNA levels at all concentrations compared to nontreated cultures (p>0.05; ANOVA, Figure 9C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9C using RT-qPCR on cultured neurons.

claim: NTSR1 was expressed at the plasma membrane of CA1 pyramidal neuron cell bodies in vivo.
source: NTSR1 was expressed at the plasma membrane of CA1 cell bodies (arrowheads in Figure 12D and F), consistent with the cell membrane localization of NTSR1
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 12 using immunohistochemistry.

claim: NTSR1 was expressed within proximal dendrites of pyramidal neurons in vivo.
source: as well as within proximal dendrites of pyramidal neurons (arrows in Figure 12D and F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 12 using immunohistochemistry.

claim: Dendritic protuberances reminiscent of dendritic spines were highly immunolabeled for NTSR1 in vivo.
source: Note that similar to transfection results and immunocytochemistry on mature cultured neurons, the dendritic protuberances, reminiscent of dendritic spines, were also highly immunolabeled for NTSR1 (arrowheads in Figure 12D high-magnification inset).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 12 using immunohistochemistry.

claim: VH-N412 at 1 and 10 µM significantly protects hippocampal neurons from NMDA-induced cell death compared to control.
source: VH-N412 at 1 and 10 µM protects significantly hippocampal neurons from NMDA-induced cell death compared to control (75.66% and 70.28% of the CTL, respectively, p<0.05, Dunnett's test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 13B using in vitro neuronal survival assays.

claim: The neuroprotective effects of VH-N412 against NMDA-induced cell death are as potent as those of BDNF.
source: These effects of VH-N412 were as potent as those of BDNF (50 ng/mL) (72.28% of the CTL, p<0.05, Dunnett's test), used as a well-known neuroprotective molecule following NMDA intoxication (Mattson et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 13B comparing VH-N412 to BDNF.

claim: Antagonizing NTSR with SR142948A and SR48692 blocked the neuroprotective effects mediated by VH-N412 in rat primary neuronal cultures injured by NMDA.
source: Antagonizing NTSR with the SR142948A (0.1; 1 and 10 μM) and SR48692 (0.1 and 1 μM) NTSR antagonists blocked the neuroprotective effects mediated by VH-N412 in rat primary neuronal cultures injured by NMDA (Figure 13B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 13B using NTSR antagonists.

claim: VH-N412 at 0.1, 1, and 10 µM significantly protected hippocampal neurons from KA-induced cell death compared to control.
source: VH-N412 at 0.1, 1, and 10 µM significantly protected hippocampal neurons from KA-induced cell death compared to control (80.46%, p<0.05, 85.88%, p<0.01, 91.23%, p<0.01 of the CTL, respectively, Dunnett's test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 13C using in vitro neuronal survival assays.

claim: The neuroprotective effects of VH-N412 against KA-induced cell death are similar to those of oestradiol.
source: These effects of VH-N412 were similar to those of oestradiol (100 nM) (81.68% of the CTL, p<0.05, Dunnett's test), used as a neuroprotective molecule following KA intoxication (Kajta and Lasoń, 2000).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 13C comparing VH-N412 to oestradiol.

claim: VH-N412 had no significant effects on the total length of dendrites following KA injury.
source: In contrast to oestradiol, VH-N412 had no significant effects on the total length of dendrites following KA injury.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 13C.

claim: This is the first report describing the successful treatment of SE with PIH.
source: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report describing the successful treatment of SE with PIH.
evidence: Based on the authors' knowledge of the literature and the novelty of their findings.

claim: Vectorized NT may elicit different neuroprotection mechanisms mediated by hypothermia and/or by intrinsic neuroprotective properties.
source: In all, our results show that vectorized NT may elicit different neuroprotection mechanisms mediated by hypothermia and/or by intrinsic neuroprotective properties.
evidence: Based on the combined in vivo and in vitro experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mild to moderate hypothermia is neuroprotective in sudden cardiac arrest with resuscitation, ischemic stroke, perinatal hypoxia/ischemia, and traumatic brain injury.
source: Preclinical and clinical studies have shown that mild to moderate hypothermia is neuroprotective in situations of exacerbated neuronal death including sudden cardiac arrest with resuscitation, ischemic stroke, perinatal hypoxia/ischemia, and traumatic brain injury (TBI) (Kida et al., 2013; Andresen et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Hypothermia decreases seizure burden in experimental models.
source: Studies also suggest that hypothermia decreases seizure burden in experimental models (Sartorius and Berger, 1998; Schmitt et al., 2006; Niquet et al., 2015a; Niquet et al., 2015b)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Hypothermia decreases seizure burden in humans.
source: and in humans (Karkar et al., 2002; Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Selective brain cooling has broad-ranging anti-inflammatory effects and prevents the development of spontaneously occurring seizures in a rat model of post-traumatic epilepsy.
source: Selective brain cooling has also broad-ranging anti-inflammatory effects and prevents the development of spontaneously occurring seizures in a rat model of post-traumatic epilepsy (D'Ambrosio et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: There is a positive relationship between therapeutic hypothermia and seizures in neonates with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy.
source: Results in animal studies are supported by clinical data showing a positive relationship between therapeutic hypothermia (TH) and seizures in neonates with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (Orbach et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Mild hypothermia decreases seizure burden during and after pediatric RSE and may prevent RSE relapse.
source: Pediatric case series report treatment of refractory status epilepticus (RSE) with mild hypothermia, which decreases seizure burden during and after pediatric RSE and may prevent RSE relapse.
evidence: Supported by citations (Guilliams et al., 2013; reviewed in Ferlisi and Shorvon, 2012; Bennett et al., 2014).

claim: Hypothermia is used in several centers around the world as second-line therapy for patients with RSE, despite a small evidence base.
source: Hypothermia is also used in several centers around the world as second-line therapy for patients with RSE, despite a small evidence base (Guilliams et al., 2013; reviewed in Ferlisi and Shorvon, 2012; Bennett et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mild hypothermia is most effective for treating seizures.
source: While the level of hypothermia is uncertain, it has been suggested that mild hypothermia is most effective (Rossetti and Lowenstein, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Focal brain cooling reduces epileptic discharges and concentrations of glutamate and glycerol in patients with intractable epilepsy, suggesting neuroprotective effects.
source: Focal brain cooling also reduces epileptic discharges (EDs) and concentrations of glutamate and glycerol in patients with intractable epilepsy, suggesting neuroprotective effects (Nomura et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Physical cooling therapies induce several clinical complications, including electrolyte disturbances, coagulation dysfunction, infections, and cardiac arrhythmia.
source: Current methods for the induction of hypothermia largely involve physical cooling therapies, which induce several clinical complications, including electrolyte disturbances, coagulation dysfunction, infections, and cardiac arrhythmia (Carraway and Leeman, 1975; Carraway and Leeman, 1973).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Forced hypothermia lowers core temperature by overwhelming the body's capacity to thermoregulate, but does not change the temperature set point, thus generating counter-regulation mechanisms such as shivering and tremor.
source: In particular, forced hypothermia lowers core temperature by overwhelming the body's capacity to thermoregulate, but does not change the temperature set point, thus generating counter-regulation mechanisms such as shivering and tremor (Feketa et al., 2013; Suchomelova et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Counter-regulation mechanisms from forced hypothermia warrant sedation and curarization in intensive care units.
source: which warrant sedation and curarization in intensive care units (Andresen et al., 2015; Hammer et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Pharmacologically induced hypothermia (PIH) promotes a controlled decrease in core temperature by lowering the brain's temperature set point and maintaining thermoregulation at lower set points.
source: Pharmacologically induced hypothermia (PIH) was obtained in animal models using different molecules. They promote a controlled decrease in core temperature by lowering the brain's temperature set point and maintaining thermoregulation at lower set points (Liska et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: NT interacts with three receptor subtypes, including NTSR1, NTSR2, and gp95/Sort-1 or NTSR3, to mediate its peripheral and central effects.
source: NT interacts with three receptor subtypes, including NTSR1, NTSR2, and gp95/Sort-1 or NTSR3, to mediate its peripheral and central effects.
evidence: Supported by citations (Vincent, 1995; Mazella, 2001) as indicated in the full text.

claim: NTSR1 and NTSR2 are G protein-coupled receptors with seven transmembrane domains.
source: The G protein-coupled receptors NTSR1 and NTSR2 have seven transmembrane domains (Vincent, 1995)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Sort1/NTSR3 has one single transmembrane domain and is not coupled to a G protein.
source: while Sort1/NTSR3 only has one single transmembrane domain and is not coupled to a G protein (Mazella, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: NTSR1 shows high affinity for NT while NTSR2 shows lower affinity.
source: NTSR1 and NTSR2 differ in their affinity for NT, with NTSR1 and NTSR2 showing high and lower affinity, respectively (Tanaka et al., 1990; Chalon et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: NTSR1 is expressed prenatally, preferentially in neurons in different brain structures.
source: NTSR1 is expressed prenatally, preferentially in neurons in different brain structures (Palacios et al., 1988)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: NTSR2 is expressed postnatally, essentially in glial and endothelial cells and increases during brain development.
source: while NTSR2 is expressed postnatally, essentially in glial and endothelial cells and increases during brain development (Sarret et al., 1998; Lépée-Lorgeoux et al., 1999; Yamauchi et al., 2007; Woodworth et al., 2018; Kyriatzis et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: NT induces PIH by inducing a downward shift of the physiological temperature set point.
source: NT has been shown to induce PIH when administered intracerebrally (Coquerel et al., 1986; Coquerel et al., 1988; Popp et al., 2007; Fanelli et al., 2015), by inducing a downward shift of the physiological temperature set point (Gordon et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A number of NT analogues have been generated that are more stable than NT and that cross the BBB to induce hypothermia.
source: A number of NT analogues have been generated that are more stable than NT and that cross the BBB to induce hypothermia (reviewed in McMahon et al., 2002; Gordon et al., 2003; Orwig et al., 2009; Boules et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: NT analogues have shown significant neuroprotection in several models of acute brain damage such as hypoxic ischemia, stroke, and TBI.
source: These analogues have shown significant neuroprotection in several models of acute brain damage such as hypoxic ischemia, stroke, and TBI (Choi et al., 2012; Gu et al., 2015; Zhong et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There are no reports on the effects of PIH in epileptic discharges prior to this study.
source: However, to our knowledge, there are no reports on the effects of PIH in EDs.
evidence: Based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: Transport of active principles across the BBB can be enhanced by conjugation to ligand or 'vector' molecules designed to bind specific receptors involved in receptor-mediated transcytosis (RMT).
source: Indeed, transport of active principles across the BBB can be enhanced by conjugation to ligand or 'vector' molecules designed to bind specific receptors involved in receptor-mediated transcytosis (RMT) (Pardridge, 2001; Pardridge, 2003; de Boer and Gaillard, 2007; Jones and Shusta, 2007; Pardridge, 2007; reviewed in Vlieghe and Khrestchatisky, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Several BBB receptors have been described that undergo RMT, including the transferrin receptor, the insulin receptor, the insulin-like growth factor receptor, and receptors of the low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR) family.
source: Several BBB receptors have been described that undergo RMT, including the transferrin receptor, the insulin receptor, the insulin-like growth factor receptor, and receptors of the low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR) family.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge and citations.

claim: A number of antibodies, protein ligands, or peptides that bind some of these receptors have been developed as vectors to carry pharmacological payloads across the BBB.
source: A number of antibodies, protein ligands, or peptides that bind some of these receptors have been developed as vectors to carry pharmacological payloads across the BBB (Friden et al., 1991; Wu et al., 1997; Wu and Pardridge, 1998; Boado et al., 2007; Pan et al., 2004; Spencer and Verma, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: LDLR is part of a group of single transmembrane glycoproteins, referred to as cell surface endocytic receptors.
source: LDLR is part of a group of single transmembrane glycoproteins, referred to as cell surface endocytic receptors. They bind apolipoprotein complexes and are expressed with some degree of tissue specificity (Brown and Goldstein, 1979; Herz and Bock, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The authors previously described the rational characterization and optimization of a family of cyclic peptides that bind the LDLR in vitro and in vivo.
source: We previously described the rational characterization and optimization of a family of cyclic peptides that bind the LDLR in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: Supported by citations to the authors' prior work (Malcor et al., 2012; Jacquot et al., 2016; David et al., 2018; Varini et al., 2019; Acier et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2023; Broc et al., 2024).

claim: The LDLR-binding peptides bind the EGF-precursor homology domain of the LDLR and thus do not compete with LDL binding on the ligand-binding domain.
source: These peptides bind the EGF-precursor homology domain of the LDLR and thus do not compete with LDL binding on the ligand-binding domain.
evidence: Supported by the authors' prior research.

claim: The LDLR-binding peptides have no beneficial or untoward effects on LDL binding and LDLR activity.
source: To our knowledge, they have no beneficial or untoward effects on LDL binding and LDLR activity (Malcor et al., 2012; Jacquot et al., 2016; David et al., 2018; Varini et al., 2019; Acier et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2023; Broc et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to the authors' prior work.

claim: The LDLR-binding peptides can transport across the BBB and into the CNS and specific organs, different payloads in an LDLR-dependent manner.
source: These peptides can transport across the BBB and into the CNS and specific organs, different payloads in an LDLR-dependent manner.
evidence: Supported by citations to the authors' and others' prior work.

claim: Payloads that can be transported by LDLR-binding peptides include fluorophores, proteins, nanoparticles, and liposome-based cargos.
source: We and others have shown that such payloads include fluorophores, proteins, nanoparticles, and liposome-based cargos (Malcor et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2017; Molino et al., 2017; Cui et al., 2018; David et al., 2018; Shen et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The FVB/N mouse strain is a reliable and well-described mouse model of epilepsy, where seizures are associated with cell death and inflammation.
source: This mouse strain was selected as a reliable and well-described mouse model of epilepsy, where seizures are associated with cell death and neuroinflammation (Schauwecker, 2003; Wu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Temporal lobe epilepsy is associated with sprouting of the mossy fibers in the inner molecular layer, in response to hilar cell loss.
source: Temporal lobe epilepsy is associated with sprouting of the mossy fibers in the inner molecular layer (IML), in response to hilar cell loss (Jiao and Nadler, 2007; Sloviter et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Epilepsy is associated with learning and memory difficulties in patients and animal models.
source: Epilepsy is associated with learning and memory difficulties in patients and animal models (Giovagnoli and Avanzini, 1999; Löscher and Stafstrom, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Cold shock proteins such as RBM3 and CIRBP are involved in diverse physiological and pathological processes, including circadian rhythm, inflammation, neural plasticity, stem cell properties, and cancer development.
source: Cold shock proteins such as the RNA-binding protein RBM3 and cold-inducible RNA-binding protein (CIRBP) are involved in diverse physiological and pathological processes, including circadian rhythm, inflammation, neural plasticity, stem cell properties, and cancer development (reviewed in Zhu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior review.

claim: Cooling and hibernation in animals induces expression of RBM3 and CIRBP.
source: In particular, cooling and hibernation in animals induces expression of RBM3 and CIRBP (Shiina and Shimizu, 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Boosting endogenous RBM3 levels through hypothermia is neuroprotective.
source: and boosting endogenous RBM3 levels through hypothermia is neuroprotective (Ávila-Gómez et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: NT enhanced glutamate-induced excitotoxicity through NTSR1 activation in both mesencephalic and cortical neurons.
source: NT enhanced glutamate-induced excitotoxicity through NTSR1 activation in both mesencephalic and cortical neurons (Antonelli et al., 2004; Antonelli et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: NT increased glutamate release in some brain regions.
source: NT increased glutamate release in some brain regions (Sanz et al., 1993; Ferraro et al., 1995)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In addition to enhancing glutamate release, NT can modify the function of glutamate receptors in vitro and in vivo.
source: and it has been shown that in addition to enhancing glutamate release, NT can modify the function of glutamate receptors in vitro and in vivo (Antonelli et al., 2004; Ferraro et al., 2011; Ferraro et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The maximal tolerated dose of VH-N412 was >40 mg/kg eq. NT in naïve mice.
source: We thus report a very interesting therapeutic index since the maximal tolerated dose was >40 mg/kg eq. NT
evidence: Supported by tolerability studies described in the manuscript.

claim: The maximum hypothermic effect of VH-N412 is observed at a 10× lower dose than the maximal tolerated dose.
source: while the maximum effect is observed at a 10× lower dose of 4 mg/kg eq. NT
evidence: Supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The ED50 of VH-N412 was established at 0.69 mg/kg.
source: and an ED50 established at 0.69 mg/kg as shown in Figure 1G.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Severe hypothermia could be induced in rats with different conjugates similar to VH-N412 with the same efficacy and safety.
source: Severe hypothermia could also be induced in rats with different conjugates similar to VH-N412 with the same efficacy and safety (data not shown).
evidence: Based on unpublished data mentioned by the authors.
